questions.prompt: What does closure mean in relational algebra?
options: The output is always a number
Every query has only one operator
The output is a relation that another operator can use
questions.explanation: Returning relations enables composition. An operator such as projection can still change the schema.

questions.prompt: What is an important difference between pure RA and default SQL?
options: RA uses sets; SQL normally uses bags
RA uses only strings; SQL uses only integers
RA requires sorting; SQL forbids it
questions.explanation: The difference concerns multiplicity, not numeric types or the existence of joins.

questions.prompt: How does a physical plan differ from a logical plan?
options: A logical plan gives only the final result and contains no operators
A physical plan chooses specific execution algorithms
A physical plan may change query semantics to run faster
A logical plan already fixes every individual I/O
questions.explanation: A logical operator describes a transformation. A physical operator chooses how to perform it while preserving its semantics.

questions.prompt: Why can RA schema validity be checked before execution?
options: The output schema is known only after every value has been examined
Operators always preserve the schema, so no check is needed
An operator’s input schemas determine its output schema
All relations must have the same schema
questions.explanation: The typed structure supports static checks. It does not imply that all relations are schema-compatible.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of connecting calculus and algebra in this lecture?
options: To prove that equivalent plans always have the same runtime
To guarantee that every query runs without I/O
To guarantee that every query needs only one operator
To connect declarative descriptions with operational transformations
questions.explanation: Their connection in expressive power supports query compilation. It does not guarantee constant execution time.

questions.prompt: For R(x)={1,3,5}, what is σ x>2(R)?
questions.explanation: Selection retains tuples satisfying the predicate. It does not create the boundary value 2.

questions.prompt: What does selection primarily affect?
options: Multiplicity is multiplied by the number of conditions
questions.explanation: Selection filters tuples while retaining the input schema. Projection selects columns.

questions.prompt: For R(x,y)={(1,8),(3,4),(3,9)}, which rows satisfy x=3 AND y>5?
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions to hold. Satisfying x=3 alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: For the same R, which rows satisfy x=1 OR y=4?
questions.explanation: OR requires at least one condition to be true, not both simultaneously.

questions.prompt: Can selection increase the number of tuples in a set relation?
options: Yes, if its predicate contains OR
Yes, if there are two conditions
Yes, if all columns are retained
questions.explanation: Each input tuple is either retained once or discarded. OR does not multiply tuples.

questions.prompt: For R(a,b)={(1,2),(1,3),(4,5)}, what is π a(R) in set RA?
questions.explanation: Projection retains a, and set semantics eliminate duplicate tuples. SQL without DISTINCT can retain both occurrences of 1.

questions.prompt: Must projection reduce the tuple count?
options: Yes; exactly one row always remains
No; it always preserves duplicates like a bag
No; the projected values may remain distinct
Yes; at least one row must disappear
questions.explanation: Projection can reduce or preserve cardinality. It need not make any two rows identical.

questions.prompt: How many columns are in the output schema of π a,c applied to R(a,b,c)?
options: The number of rows in R
questions.explanation: The projection list contains two attributes. Input row count does not determine schema width.

questions.prompt: When can SELECT a FROM R and π a(R) have different cardinalities?
options: When several R tuples have the same a value
questions.explanation: SQL bag projection does not automatically eliminate duplicates; set projection does.

questions.prompt: Why is duplicate elimination not considered free in a database system?
options: Schema metadata always identifies every duplicate exactly
It takes work to identify and remove duplicate result tuples
SQL projection already eliminates all duplicates automatically
Dropping a column is sufficient to eliminate duplicates
questions.explanation: Deduplication requires processing. This does not mean that the source data must be modified or deleted.

questions.prompt: For A={1,2} and B={2,3}, what is A∪B?
questions.explanation: Set union retains every value that appears, but does not retain a duplicate 2.

questions.prompt: What basic requirement must hold to union two relations?
options: They must contain the same number of tuples
They must have no values in common
They must have the same number of fields with compatible corresponding types
questions.explanation: Schema compatibility concerns columns and types, not cardinality or indexes.

questions.prompt: For bags A=[1,2] and B=[2,3], how many rows does SQL UNION ALL return?
questions.explanation: UNION ALL preserves both inputs’ multiplicities. UNION performs duplicate elimination.

questions.prompt: Can A(a:int,b:text) and B(x:int) be unioned directly under the lecture’s rules?
options: Yes, if x is renamed a
No; they have different numbers of fields
Yes, because their first fields are both int
Yes, if B has fewer rows
questions.explanation: Renaming does not supply the missing field. Union requires equal schema width.

questions.prompt: How does set A∪A compare with A?
options: It contains only one arbitrary tuple
It has twice as many tuples
questions.explanation: Set union is idempotent. Bag concatenation or UNION ALL would double multiplicities.

questions.prompt: For A={1,2,4} and B={2,3}, what is A−B?
questions.explanation: Keep tuples in A that are not in B. The set {3} is B−A instead.

questions.prompt: Is set difference commutative?
options: No; A−B generally differs from B−A
Yes, when the sets have equal size
questions.explanation: The direction determines which input supplies retained tuples. Equal types or sizes do not make difference symmetric.

questions.prompt: What is the result of A−A?
options: An empty relation with the same schema
questions.explanation: Every A tuple is also in the subtracted set. No tuples remain, but the schema is still defined.

questions.prompt: Which SQL operator does the deck associate with set difference?
questions.explanation: EXCEPT expresses set difference. An inner join finds matching pairs rather than subtracting tuples.

questions.prompt: For A={(1,a),(1,b)} and B={(1,a)}, what remains in A−B?
questions.explanation: Set comparison uses the whole tuple. Sharing the first field 1 does not remove every such tuple.

questions.prompt: R has 4 tuples and S has 3. How many tuples are in R×S?
questions.explanation: Every R tuple combines with every S tuple, giving 4×3 rather than their sum.

questions.prompt: R has 5 tuples and S is empty. How many tuples are in their product?
questions.explanation: No pairs exist when one input is empty: 5×0=0.

questions.prompt: R has 2 columns and S has 3. How many fields does their product contain before projection?
questions.explanation: The product combines both tuples’ fields, so column counts are added. Row-pair counts are multiplied.

questions.prompt: Does a product require union-compatible input schemas?
options: Yes; the inputs need equal tuple counts
Yes; at least one field name must be shared
questions.explanation: A product can combine tuples with different schemas. Union compatibility is required for set operations such as union.

questions.prompt: For R(a)={1,2} and S(b)={x,y}, which tuples belong to their product?
questions.explanation: A product creates every pair. It does not pair rows by matching positions.

questions.prompt: What does the rename operator change directly?
options: A relation name or attribute names
The value of the renamed field
The tuples retained by a predicate
questions.explanation: Rename changes names. It neither changes data values nor filters rows.

questions.prompt: Why are aliases useful when self-joining two copies of Employee?
options: They automatically turn the self-join into a union
They ensure the two copies contain different data
They distinguish fields belonging to two different roles
They automatically remove pairs with identical ids
questions.explanation: Two copies with the same schema need unambiguous references. Aliasing is neither deduplication nor indexing.

questions.prompt: R(a,b)={(1,2)} is renamed so that a becomes x. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Renaming an attribute preserves its values and the other columns. It does not turn the name into a data value.

questions.prompt: R×S contains two fields named id. Which approach expresses them unambiguously?
options: Automatically add the two ids together
Discard every tuple with nonmatching names
questions.explanation: Rename removes ambiguity while retaining information. Projection or addition would be different transformations.

questions.prompt: Does renaming a set relation change its cardinality?
options: Yes; renaming is equivalent to a self-product
Yes; it removes every tuple duplicated under the new name
Yes; every new name creates another tuple
questions.explanation: Rename changes only schema or relation labels. Name length does not determine the tuple count.

questions.prompt: For A={2,4,6} and B={1,4,6}, what is A∩B?
questions.explanation: Intersection retains shared tuples. Union retains every value appearing in either input.

questions.prompt: Which expression equals A∩B in set RA?
questions.explanation: Removing from A everything that is not in B leaves their shared elements.

questions.prompt: If A∩B is empty, which statement is true?
options: The relations have no identical tuples in common
At least one relation must be empty
The relations must have different column counts
A and B must have different types
questions.explanation: Two nonempty sets can be disjoint. Their schemas must still satisfy compatibility requirements.

questions.prompt: Does intersection require schema compatibility, as union does?
options: Only one shared column name is required
No; intersection examines only the first field
Only equal tuple counts are required, not compatible types
questions.explanation: Corresponding tuple positions and types must be comparable. Row counts do not remove that requirement.

questions.prompt: What is A∩A?
questions.explanation: Every tuple in A belongs to both inputs. Intersection does not select just one arbitrary tuple.

questions.prompt: Which expression is equivalent to a theta join?
questions.explanation: Semantically, a theta join is a product followed by selection. The product need not be materialised physically.

questions.prompt: Which kind of theta join is an equijoin?
options: Its predicate is a conjunction of equalities
Its predicate can be any greater-than or less-than comparison
It necessarily joins all shared names and removes repeated columns
It must join only one primary key
questions.explanation: An equijoin uses equality conditions. Removing shared columns characterises a natural join, not every equijoin.

questions.prompt: For R(x)={1,3} and S(y)={2,4}, how many pairs satisfy theta condition x<y?
questions.explanation: The qualifying pairs are (1,2),(1,4),(3,4). The pair (3,2) fails.

questions.prompt: What schema does a theta join have before projection?
options: The fields from both inputs, as in a product
questions.explanation: Selection over a product preserves the product schema. The predicate does not replace the output with one Boolean column.

questions.prompt: A self-join on ages={20,25,30} uses age_left<age_right. How many pairs result?
questions.explanation: The increasing pairs are (20,25),(20,30),(25,30). Reversed and equal-age pairs are excluded.

questions.prompt: What does a natural join remove compared with an equijoin on every shared name?
options: One copy of each shared field
Every row with a repeated primary key
questions.explanation: A natural join retains one column for each shared name. It does not remove the input-specific columns.

questions.prompt: For R(a,b)={(1,7)} and S(b,c)={(7,x),(8,y)}, what does their natural join return?
questions.explanation: Only b=7 matches. The output contains a,b,c with one copy of b.

questions.prompt: What is the output schema of the natural join of R(a,b) and S(b,c)?
questions.explanation: The shared name b appears once. Removing b entirely would also be incorrect.

questions.prompt: If both relations share the names id and status, what does a natural join require?
options: Equal id values OR equal status values
Equal id values AND equal status values
questions.explanation: Every shared field name participates in an equality condition, and those conditions are combined with AND.

questions.prompt: R(a)={1,2} and S(b)={x,y} share no column names. What is the semantics of their natural join?
questions.explanation: With no shared-name equalities to filter by, every pair satisfies the empty conjunction. This is a product, not a union.

questions.prompt: What does γ denote among the additional operators?
questions.explanation: The operator γ expresses group-based computation. Product and rename have separate operators.

questions.prompt: Under which semantics is a separate duplicate-elimination operator δ most clearly needed?
options: Only when a relation has exactly one tuple
Only when every column is unique
Set semantics, which already exclude duplicates
questions.explanation: Bags contain multiplicities that can be removed. Sets already contain no duplicate tuples.

questions.prompt: How does sorting differ from projection in purpose?
options: Sorting always reduces the column count
Sorting specifies order; projection selects fields
questions.explanation: Sorting does not select columns. Equal output cardinalities do not make the two operations equivalent.

questions.prompt: What values result from applying δ to the bag x=[2,2,5]?
questions.explanation: The operator δ removes the extra occurrence of 2 while preserving both distinct values.

questions.prompt: Apply γ dept,COUNT(*) to a bag with dept=[CS,CS,Math], then retain groups with count>1. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Grouping produces (CS,2) and (Math,1). The condition count>1 retains the CS group, not the two original CS rows.
